pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law, integer scaling problems, and harder correspondence (n×m combinations) problems.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law to multiply two-digit numbers by one digit, integer scaling problems and harder correspondence problems such as n objects are connected to m objects'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.2/4.OA.3 — multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems (including which operation and interpreting remainders); 3.OA.8 two-step problems; correspondence combinations connect to the multiplication principle of counting.
• Operational details — this is the APPLICATION topic that ties three distinct multiplicative structures together: (1) distributive-law calculation (14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6) as a mental/written strategy; (2) SCALING — 'three times as tall/heavy', a multiplicative (not additive) comparison; (3) CORRESPONDENCE / combinations — 3 breads × 4 fillings = 12 sandwiches, where multiplication counts pairings. Children must identify which structure a problem has and choose operations; the bar model and a systematic table/tree are the key tools. The recurring pitfall is reading scaling additively and mis-organising correspondence.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): solve a one-step scaling problem and a small correspondence problem with support (2×3). Tier B (age 8–9): use the distributive law on 14×6 and solve a correspondence problem by systematic listing/table. Tier C (age 9): solve a multi-step multiply-and-add problem, choosing operations and justifying with a bar model.
bestPractices: Teach the three structures explicitly and by name — distributive calculation, scaling (times-as-many), correspondence (combinations) — so children recognise which they face rather than key-word guessing.
Use the bar model as the shared representation for scaling and multiply-and-add, making the multiplicative comparison visible against an additive one.
For correspondence, build systematic organisation — a grid/table or tree diagram — so children see why you multiply the two counts rather than add them.
Contrast scaling with addition directly ('3 times as tall' vs '3 m taller') using the same numbers so the multiplicative meaning is felt.
Progress from one-step to genuinely multi-step problems, requiring an estimate and an operation choice, and checking answers for reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Bar model — scaling and multiply-and-add (unit bar × scale factor; combine bars)
Systematic table / grid — correspondence combinations (rows×columns = pairings)
Tree diagram — correspondence (each bread branches to each filling)
commonMisconceptions: Reading scaling additively — 'three times as tall as 15 m' answered as 15+3 rather than 15×3.
Adding the two counts in a correspondence problem (3+4=7 sandwiches) instead of multiplying.
Unsystematic listing of combinations, so some pairings are missed or duplicated.
Applying the distributive split incorrectly (14×6 = 10×6 + 4, dropping the second multiplication).
Relying on key words instead of the problem's structure, choosing the wrong operation in multi-step problems.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: solving multiply-and-add problems across three distinct multiplicative structures — (1) the distributive law as a calculation strategy (14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6 = 60+24 = 84); (2) scaling / multiplicative comparison ('3 times as tall as 15 m' = 45 m, NOT 15+3 = 18); and (3) correspondence / combinations (3 breads × 4 fillings = 12 sandwiches). The central aim is for learners to identify which structure a problem has and choose operations accordingly, rather than guessing from key words. Bar models and systematic tables/trees are the shared tools; the recurring pitfalls are reading scaling additively and adding the two counts in correspondence problems.

activities.title: Correspondence combinations: pair every bread with every filling
feedback: If a learner answers 7 (adding the counts), show the grid or tree: there are more than 7 cells to fill. Name it explicitly — '4 sandwiches for EACH of the 3 breads'.
If pairings are missed or duplicated, point to the empty or repeated cells and work row by row so each bread is paired with all 4 fillings exactly once.
Confirm correct reasoning by linking the completed grid back to 3 rows × 4 columns = 12.
activities.rationale: The multiplicative structure in correspondence problems is hidden, so children most often add (3+4=7). Building the pairings systematically in a grid or tree reveals why the total is a product. A draggable grid that auto-fills as each bread is paired, with a visible counter settling on 12, makes the 3×4 structure concrete — but a paper table or tree diagram achieves the same organisation. (Optional interactive: show empty cells remaining if a learner tries to add rather than pair.)
sourceClaims: Bar models and systematic tables/tree diagrams support scaling and correspondence problems; scaling should be contrasted with additive comparison to prevent the additive misconception.
learnerActions: Work with a concrete set-up of 3 kinds of bread and 4 kinds of filling (cards, drawings, or a draggable grid).
Systematically pair each bread with each filling, recording every sandwich in a table whose rows are breads and columns are fillings, or a tree where each bread branches to all 4 fillings.
After completing the pairings, count the filled cells and state the total as a number sentence: 3 × 4 = 12.
Explain in words why it is 3×4 and not 3+4: 'each of the 3 breads makes 4 sandwiches.'
Predict then check: 'If there were 5 fillings instead of 4, how many sandwiches now?' (3 × 5 = 15).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication counts pairings. When n objects each connect to m objects, the total number of combinations is n×m, not n+m. A systematic grid or tree makes every pairing visible so none are missed or duplicated.

activities.title: Scaling vs adding: 'times as tall' against 'taller by'
feedback: If a learner answers 18 for 'times as tall', show that they added the multiplier; 'times as tall' means making copies — lay out three 15 m bars and count.
Reinforce by asking the learner to re-read the phrase and decide: copies (×) or an amount extra (+)?
Confirm 3 × 15 = 45 m and have them point to the three stacked bars.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting the scaling and additive readings with identical numbers targets the common additive-scaling error. The bar model makes the multiplicative comparison visible. (Optional interactive: a bar that stretches ×n beside a faint '+n' bar so 45 towers over 18.)
sourceClaims: Bar models and systematic tables/tree diagrams support scaling and correspondence problems; scaling should be contrasted with additive comparison to prevent the additive misconception.
4.OA.2/4.OA.3 require multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems including choosing operations; correspondence problems connect to the multiplication counting principle.
learnerActions: Draw or build a bar representing a 15 m building.
Make the tower '3 times as tall' by building three copies of the 15 m bar stacked end to end, and compute 3 × 15 = 45 m.
Alongside it, build a second comparison: '3 m taller than 15 m' = 15 + 3 = 18 m.
Place the two results side by side and describe the difference between 'times as tall' (multiplicative) and 'taller by' (additive).
State which phrase means multiply and which means add, using the same numbers so the contrast is felt.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Times as many/tall/heavy' is a multiplicative comparison (copies of the original), fundamentally different from 'more than / taller by', which is additive. The same numbers give very different answers (45 vs 18).

activities.title: Distributive law: split, multiply both parts, recombine
feedback: If a learner gives 60 or 64 (only the 10 multiplied, or 4 added without multiplying), return to the area model: the 4-strip must also be multiplied by 6, giving 24, before adding.
Note that the two partial products here are 60 and 24, which sum to 84; check both are present.
If the set-up is right but the arithmetic slips, do not reteach the structure — have the learner recompute and estimate to catch the slip.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is splitting the distributive calculation but multiplying only one part (14×6 = 10×6 + 4). The area/partition model shows both strips must be multiplied and combined. Self-audit: 10×6=60 and 4×6=24 sum to 84; the partial products are 60 and 24.
learnerActions: Split 14 into 10 + 4.
Multiply BOTH parts by 6: 10 × 6 = 60 and 4 × 6 = 24.
Add the two partial products: 60 + 24 = 84.
Use an area/partition model — a rectangle split into a 10-strip and a 4-strip, both ×6 — to show both pieces are included.
Check the result is reasonable (e.g. 14×6 is a bit more than 10×6 = 60, and less than 15×6 = 90).
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive law lets you multiply a two-digit number by splitting it, but every part of the split must be multiplied by the second factor and then added. Dropping a partial product gives a wrong answer.

activities.title: Which structure is it? Classify and choose the operation
feedback: If a learner relies on a key word and picks the wrong operation, ask what the problem is really doing — making copies (scaling), counting pairings (correspondence), or splitting a calculation (distributive)?
For multi-step problems, check the estimate against the final answer for reasonableness.
Praise justifications that name the structure and match it to a representation, not just correct numbers.
activities.rationale: Progressing from one-step to multi-step problems and requiring operation choice plus an estimate builds the habit of structural reasoning over key-word matching. Classification and matching number-sentence tasks are good for checking recognition, but should accompany, not replace, building the intuition with bars and grids — recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the pairings or the comparison.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.2/4.OA.3 require multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems including choosing operations; correspondence problems connect to the multiplication counting principle.
learnerActions: Read a mix of word problems and sort each into its structure: distributive calculation, scaling (times-as-many), or correspondence (combinations) — and some multi-step multiply-and-add problems.
For each, write the number sentence before computing, justifying why that operation fits the structure.
Tackle at least one genuinely multi-step problem that needs an operation choice and a combine step; estimate first, then compute and check for reasonableness.
Explain your choice using a bar model (for scaling/multiply-and-add) or a table/tree (for correspondence).
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing operations should come from recognising the problem's structure, not from hunting for key words. The same operation (multiplication) appears in three disguises; identifying the structure drives the correct set-up.

activities.title: Talk it through: what is this problem really asking?
feedback: If the learner is unsure, redirect to a quick table or drawing to ground the discussion in visible pairings.
When they say 'one more filling gives 3 more sandwiches (one per bread)', confirm they are reasoning about the structure, not a memorised rule.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue supports problem-parsing habits and surfaces a learner's thinking. It complements, rather than replaces, the manipulable bars and grids where the structures are most clearly seen.
learnerActions: With a partner or adult playing a sandwich-shop owner, discuss a correspondence problem aloud: 'How many different sandwiches can I make?'
Answer probing questions: 'Are we making copies, or pairing options? If I add one more filling, how many MORE sandwiches — and why that many?'
Articulate the reasoning in your own words before writing a number sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Parsing a word problem aloud — distinguishing 'times as many' from 'how many pairs' — builds the habit of interpreting structure before computing.

constraints: Classification and multiple-choice tasks verify whether a learner recognises structure but do not require them to construct the pairings or the comparison themselves; pair them with building activities.

Static worked panels (a scaling bar, a filled grid, a distributive split) are useful anchors for recognising structure, but they do not let the learner build the pairings or experience the multiplicative-vs-additive contrast dynamically; treat them as reference scaffolds.
Paper/card cards and cutouts are good concrete stand-ins for breads and fillings; a screen grid is an alternative, not a requirement.
Discussion activities develop parsing habits but should be grounded in a visible table, tree, or bar so reasoning stays concrete.

Incorrect answer options in any check (e.g. 18 for '3 times as tall as 15 m', 7 for correspondence, 60/64 for the distributive split) must target the real misconceptions; do not offer arithmetically incoherent options as plausible answers.

Differentiate by readiness: less-confident/younger learners can start with a smaller correspondence set (e.g. 2×3) and a one-step scaling problem with support, progressing to the distributive calculation with systematic listing and then to multi-step multiply-and-add problems justified with a bar model.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6 = 60 + 24 = 84 (correct); the partial products are 60 and 24. 3×15 = 45 (correct); '3 m taller' = 18. 3×4 = 12 correspondence (correct); 3×5 = 15 for the 5-fillings extension. No arithmetic errors found.

The source's distributive error-pattern notes answers of '60 or 64' for splitting only one part — 60 (forgetting 4×6 entirely) and 64 (adding 4 un-multiplied) are both coherent error accounts and are preserved as diagnostic feedback, not as valid answers.

sourceClaims were pruned where an exact-copy claim supported only the curriculum topic rather than the activity's teaching principle: the DfE claim is not used on the correspondence activity (NCETM retained as the principle support) and the distributive activity has [] because no source[].claim directly supports the 'multiply both parts' area-model principle.

The CCSS-M 4.OA claim is retained on the scaling and classify activities on the basis of direct content overlap (multiplicative comparison; multistep problems with operation choice); its role as partly curriculum-scope and its verified:false status are flagged as uncertain rather than treated as established efficacy.
The original checkpoint tiering (Tier A age 8, Tier B, Tier C age 9) was folded into a differentiation constraint rather than dropped.

The legacy source's catalog-fit comparisons (3D 'adds cost', quiz 'verifies rather than builds') were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements; no comparative-efficacy or medium-superiority claim is asserted beyond the objective point that recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction.
One source claim (CCSS-M 4.OA) and the NCETM guidance claim are marked verified:false in the source; treat their support as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: For the sandwiches, why do you multiply 3 by 4 instead of adding them?
In 14 × 6, did you multiply BOTH the 10 and the 4 by 6?
'3 times as tall as 15 m' — how is that different from '3 m taller'?
If there were 5 fillings instead of 4, how many sandwiches now?
assess.correctAnswer: 84 (10×6 + 4×6 = 60 + 24); 45 m (3 × 15); 12 sandwiches (3 × 4). The teacher watches for splitting both parts in the distributive item, multiplying for scaling, and recognising the correspondence problem as a product of the two option-sets, not a sum.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds instead of multiplying on the correspondence problem (3 + 4 = 7 sandwiches)
errorPatterns.nextMove: make a systematic grid/table of bread × filling so all 12 pairings are visible; name it as '4 sandwiches for EACH of the 3 breads'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 7; child sums the two option-sets rather than pairing every bread with every filling

errorPatterns.pattern: splits only one part in the distributive method (10×6 = 60, forgets 4×6) giving 60 or 64
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the area model — both the 10-strip and the 4-strip must be multiplied by 6 and added.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: distributive answer missing a partial product

errorPatterns.pattern: reads scaling additively — '3 times as tall as 15' as 15 + 3 = 18
errorPatterns.nextMove: build three copies of the 15 m height; 'times as tall' means copies, not 'taller by'.

errorPatterns.pattern: correct set-up, arithmetic slip in a partial product or product
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach structure; have the child recompute and estimate.

responseLevels.gap: adds on the correspondence problem, splits one part in distributive, or reads scaling additively.
responseLevels.full: recognises and correctly sets up multiplication across distributive, scaling and correspondence problems, justifying why each is a product, and checks the results.
responseLevels.partial: handles the familiar distributive/scaling items but adds on correspondence, or needs prompting to see the multiplicative structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three problems to solve while you watch the method: (distributive) 'Work out 14 × 6 by splitting 14 into 10 and 4'; (scaling) 'A model tower is 3 times as tall as a 15 m building — how tall is the model?'; (correspondence) 'There are 3 kinds of bread and 4 kinds of filling. How many different sandwiches can you make?' Watch how they set up each — especially whether they multiply for correspondence rather than add.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Correspondence problems are where children most often add (3 + 4 = 7) instead of multiplying, because the multiplicative structure is hidden. Watching all three problem types shows whether the child recognises multiplication across distributive, scaling AND correspondence structures — the same operation wearing three disguises.
